The Big Step Up: Choosing Your First Unrestricted Tourer

Passing your full motorcycle test is a milestone moment. The temptation to leap straight onto the most powerful bike you can afford is strong, but the smartest approach is a measured upgrade that builds on the skills you developed during your A2 years. The best first unrestricted tourer should feel exciting but not overwhelming.

How Much Power Do You Need?

After riding at 47bhp, anything over 100bhp feels genuinely quick. The jump from 47bhp to 170bhp is dramatic and potentially dangerous if you are not prepared. A sensible upgrade path moves from 47bhp to the 70-120bhp range, then considers higher-powered machines after a year or two of unrestricted experience.

Best First Unrestricted Touring Bikes

Yamaha Tracer 9 GT — The natural upgrade from the Tracer 7. The CP3 triple produces 117bhp — a significant jump from 47bhp but delivered in a manageable, linear way. Semi-active suspension, comprehensive electronics, and excellent touring capability at an outstanding price.

Triumph Tiger 900 GT — The triple engine produces 93bhp in a characterful, accessible delivery. Not overwhelming power but enough to feel genuinely exciting after A2 restriction. The chassis is confidence-inspiring and the touring capability is excellent.

Yamaha Tenere 700 (unrestricted) — If you had a restricted Tenere, simply removing the restriction unlocks the full 72bhp. This is the most conservative upgrade and arguably the smartest — you already know the bike and the extra power transforms the motorway experience without changing the familiar handling.

Honda NT1100 — 98bhp from the Africa Twin-derived parallel twin. Smooth, manageable power with shaft drive and DCT automatic option. The NT1100 is designed to be approachable and its touring capability is superb.

BMW F 900 XR — 105bhp from the parallel twin. Sharp handling and comprehensive electronics provide a sporting touring experience that rewards developing skills. Managing the Power Jump

  • Use rain mode initially — Most modern bikes have rain or road modes that soften throttle response. Start in rain mode to acclimatise to the extra power.
  • Take an advanced riding course — IAM, RoSPA, or a private instructor will help you exploit the extra performance safely.
  • Build up gradually — Resist the urge to explore the full power on day one. Spend a month getting comfortable before pushing harder.
  • Keep your A2 bike for a month — Some riders sell their A2 bike before buying the replacement. Keep it for a few weeks of overlap so you have a familiar fallback.
The riders who transition from A2 to full licence most safely are those who treat it as a progression, not a revolution. Your A2 years built valuable skills — now build on those skills with a measured increase in power rather than a leap to the maximum.

faq.q: How much power should my first full-licence bike have?
faq.a: A sensible upgrade moves from 47bhp to the 70 to 120bhp range, then considers more powerful machines after a year or two of unrestricted experience. Jumping straight from 47bhp to 170bhp is dramatic and potentially dangerous if you are not prepared. Bikes like the Tracer 9 GT at 117bhp or Tiger 900 GT at 93bhp feel genuinely exciting without being overwhelming.

faq.q: What is the safest way to upgrade?
faq.a: The most conservative route is simply to remove the restrictor from a bike you already own, such as a restricted Tenere 700, unlocking its full 72bhp while keeping familiar handling. Otherwise, choose a mid-power bike, start in rain or road mode to soften throttle response, build up gradually over a month, and consider an advanced course with IAM or RoSPA.

faq.q: Will 100bhp feel too fast after an A2 bike?
faq.a: It will feel very quick at first, because after riding at 47bhp anything over 100bhp is a big step. That is exactly why a measured jump to the 70 to 120bhp range is recommended, with the power delivered in a linear, manageable way. Use rain mode initially, resist exploring full throttle on day one, and give yourself a month to acclimatise.

faq.q: Should I keep my A2 bike after upgrading?
faq.a: Keeping it for a few weeks of overlap is wise. Rather than selling your A2 bike before buying the replacement, retain it briefly so you have a familiar fallback while you get comfortable with the extra power. This eases the transition and means you are never forced to ride the more powerful bike before you feel ready. Sell the old bike once confidence is established.
